blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Validity is the degree to which an instrument measures the construct it claims to measure, rather than something else.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Imagine a “satisfaction questionnaire” that mostly asks about waiting time. It may give a perfectly consistent score, but that score measures “perceived waiting time”, not the broader construct it claims. Validity asks whether the instrument hits the target construct or something next to it.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A weighing scale that consistently reads 2 kg too high gives the same wrong answer every time. It is reliable but not valid: it does not measure true weight. §16.4 develops this contrast.

points.html: Validity asks “are we measuring the right thing?” Reliability (§16.3) asks “are we measuring it consistently?” An instrument can satisfy one without the other.

Four kinds of validity evidence follow: content (§16.2.1), face (§16.2.2), criterion (§16.2.3) and construct (§16.2.4). No single kind is enough. A well-validated instrument gathers evidence of several kinds, in the order set out in §16.7.

blocks.html: Content Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Content validity is the degree to which an instrument’s items cover every relevant domain of the construct, without leaving out important dimensions or including irrelevant ones.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The WHOQOL-BREF, the short form of the WHO quality-of-life instrument, scores four domains: physical health, psychological, social relationships and environment (WHOQOL Group, 1998). A quality-of-life questionnaire with content validity must touch each domain its framework defines. Leaving one out under-represents the construct, however well the other items are written.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A “quality of life” questionnaire that asks only about physical symptoms, with nothing on social relationships or psychological well-being, lacks content validity. It measures something closer to “physical symptom burden”.

points.html: Assessed by expert judgement: a panel reviews each item against a defined content domain (taken from the literature or a theoretical framework) and rates its relevance and the overall coverage.
It is judgement-based evidence, gathered during questionnaire design, before data collection.
It is necessary but not sufficient. An item’s presence does not guarantee it works once fielded.

blocks.html: Face Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Face validity is the degree to which an instrument appears, on surface inspection by ordinary (often non-expert) reviewers, to measure what it claims to.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Face validity asks only whether the questionnaire looks right to someone glancing at it. It is judged by intuition, not by a systematic or statistical process. It still matters: respondents who feel the questions make sense are more likely to answer honestly and completely.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A “Diabetes Knowledge Assessment” that visibly asks about blood sugar, insulin and diet has strong face validity, even before any expert review or statistical testing.

points.html: The weakest validity evidence: surface appearance, not systematic expert review (content validity) or data (criterion and construct validity).
Poor face validity can reduce cooperation. Respondents who cannot see why a question is asked may answer carelessly or refuse.
Content validity is a systematic, expert check of domain coverage. Face validity is “does this look reasonable?”, and anyone can judge it.

questions.prompt: A new depression screening questionnaire for elderly rural patients is adapted word-for-word from a validated questionnaire for urban working-age adults, without any local review. Which type of validity is most directly at risk, and why?
questions.answer: Content validity: whether the items cover the construct fully and appropriately for this population. The way depression shows itself, the idioms used to describe it and the relevant life domains differ by age and culture. Items about work stress may not apply to elderly rural patients, and locally common expressions of distress (for example, bodily complaints) may be missing. An expert and community review, with cultural adaptation (§16.7), is needed before use.

questions.prompt: A clinician glances at a new anxiety scale and says “these questions look like they measure anxiety.” Which more limited type of validity does this comment support?
questions.answer: Face validity only: a surface impression that the instrument appears to measure what it claims. It is weaker than content validity, which needs a systematic expert review of whether the items cover the whole construct.

blocks.html: Criterion Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Criterion validity is the degree to which scores from an instrument agree with an external, independently measured standard (the criterion) for the same or a closely related construct.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Criterion validity asks a direct, testable question: does the new score line up with an already-trusted measurement of the same thing? The statistic depends on the data. For two continuous scores, use a correlation (recall §11.2 for Pearson’s r, §11.3 for Spearman’s rank correlation). When the criterion is a yes/no diagnosis, use sensitivity, specificity and the area under the ROC curve (recall §5.5.1 and §15.5.1). When the question is whether a new method can replace the old one, use agreement statistics: kappa for categories (§16.3.3.1, which corrects agreement for chance) or limits of agreement for continuous readings (§16.3.5, the range expected to contain 95% of the differences between the two methods).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Scores on a quick depression screening questionnaire are compared with the diagnosis from a long, established clinical interview given to the same patients. Close agreement is criterion validity evidence for the quick tool.

points.html: It needs a trusted criterion. For many new constructs none exists, and criterion validity cannot be assessed.
It comes in two forms, set apart by timing: concurrent (§16.2.3.1) and predictive (§16.2.3.2).

blocks.html: Concurrent Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Concurrent validity is criterion validity with the criterion measured at about the same time as the new instrument.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: It asks whether a quicker, cheaper or newer instrument agrees with the gold standard now, on the same patients. No waiting for a future outcome is needed.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A brief anxiety screening tool and a long clinical anxiety interview are given to the same 100 patients on the same day, and the two sets of scores are correlated.

points.html: The usual evidence when a shorter, cheaper or less invasive alternative to a burdensome gold standard is being developed.

blocks.html: Predictive Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Predictive validity is criterion validity with the criterion (typically a future outcome) measured later.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: It asks whether a score measured today predicts something that happens later. That is the whole purpose of a screening or risk-prediction tool.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A screening tool is given to 200 pregnant women at their first antenatal visit to predict postpartum depression. Three months after delivery, 30 have postpartum depression on a clinical interview. Of these 30, 24 had screened positive. Of the 170 who did not develop it, 34 had screened positive.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Sensitivity = 24 ÷ 30 = 0.80 (recall §5.5.1).
  2. Specificity = (170 − 34) ÷ 170 = 136 ÷ 170 = 0.80.
  3. Of the 58 women who screened positive, 24 developed depression: PPV = 24 ÷ 58 = 0.41. Of the 142 who screened negative, 136 did not: NPV = 136 ÷ 142 = 0.96.

The binary criterion calls for sensitivity and specificity, not r. If the tool gives a continuous score, the ROC curve and its AUC (recall §15.5.1) summarise predictive validity across every cut-off.

points.html: It needs longitudinal follow-up, so it costs more time and money than concurrent validation.

With a binary future outcome, report sensitivity, specificity, predictive values or AUC. A relative risk (high scorers against low scorers) is also used. Correlation is used only when the future criterion is continuous.

blocks.html: Construct Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Construct validity is the degree to which an instrument’s scores behave as the theory of the construct predicts: they relate to other measures, differ between groups and hang together internally in the ways the theory expects.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Without a single gold standard, you test the instrument against a web of predictions made before looking at the data. Terwee et al. (2007) put it this way: construct validity “should be assessed by testing predefined hypotheses concerning the concepts that are being measured.” The COSMIN consensus places three strands under it: structural validity (does the factor structure match the theory; §16.5), hypotheses testing, and cross-cultural validity (Mokkink et al., 2010). Hypotheses testing has two common forms:

  • Correlational hypotheses: strong correlation with measures of the same or related constructs, weaker correlation with measures of related but distinct constructs (§16.2.4.1).
  • Known-groups hypotheses: the instrument “can discriminate between two groups known to differ on the variable of interest” (Davidson, 2014).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A new Hindi health-literacy questionnaire is tested against four predefined hypotheses. (1) It will correlate strongly (r > 0.6) with an established health-literacy tool. (2) It will correlate only moderately (r 0.3–0.5) with a general reading-ability test, because reading is related to health literacy but distinct from it. (3) ASHA workers will score higher than women from the same villages who have no health training. (4) Principal component analysis (§16.5: a method that finds the few weighted combinations of items that carry most of their shared variation) will show one dominant dimension. Each confirmed hypothesis adds evidence. A correlation of 0.9 with reading ability would count against the instrument: it would suggest the questionnaire measures reading, not health literacy.

points.html: Construct validity is built up across several studies, not settled by one test.
Write the hypotheses down, with expected directions and magnitudes, before analysis. Post hoc “confirmation” is weak evidence.
In the modern view (COSMIN), content, criterion and construct evidence all serve one question: do the scores mean what we claim?

blocks.html: Convergent and Discriminant Validity

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Convergent validity is evidence that an instrument correlates strongly with other measures of the same or closely related constructs. Discriminant (divergent) validity is evidence that it correlates only weakly, or less strongly, with measures of related but distinct constructs. They are two strands of construct validity. Known-groups and structural evidence are others.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Convergent validity is the “should correlate” half. Discriminant validity is the “should not correlate as much” half. The test of discriminant validity is only informative against a construct that could plausibly be confused with yours. A health-literacy score that does not correlate with height proves nothing, because nobody thought it might. A health-literacy score that correlates much less with general reading ability than with another health-literacy tool shows that the instrument is not just a reading test.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A new medication adherence scale correlates at r = 0.62 with pharmacy refill records (convergent). It correlates at r = 0.25 with a general health-beliefs scale, a related but distinct construct that it might have been confused with (discriminant). Together these support the claim that the scale measures adherence, not a broader attitude to health.

points.html: Convergent evidence alone cannot rule out the possibility that the instrument measures some broader characteristic that also correlates with the criterion.
Choose comparison constructs for discriminant validity that a critic could reasonably confuse with yours.

questions.prompt: A new physical activity scale correlates at r = 0.85 with an existing validated physical activity scale, and at r = −0.30 with a sedentary-behaviour screen (a related but distinct construct). Which strand of validity does each finding support? Why is the second comparison more informative than a correlation with shoe size would be?
questions.answer: The r = 0.85 with another physical-activity measure supports convergent validity. The much weaker r = −0.30 with a sedentary-behaviour screen supports discriminant validity: the new scale is not simply the reverse of “sitting”. Both are strands of construct validity. Sedentary behaviour is a construct a critic could plausibly confuse with physical activity, so a clear gap between 0.85 and a correlation of only −0.30 is informative. Nobody expects physical activity to track shoe size, so a near-zero correlation with it would confirm nothing.

questions.prompt: A new scale to predict medication adherence correlates well with adherence measured six months later. Which form of validity is this, and how does it differ from correlating with adherence measured on the same day?
questions.answer: Predictive validity: the criterion is measured in the future. Correlation with adherence measured at the same time would be concurrent validity. Both are forms of criterion validity, told apart by when the criterion is measured.

questions.prompt: A tool predicting low birthweight is given at 20 weeks to 250 women. Of 40 babies later born under 2.5 kg, 30 mothers had screened positive; of 210 others, 42 had screened positive. Compute the sensitivity and specificity. Why are these reported instead of r?
questions.answer:
1. Sensitivity = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75.
  2. Specificity = (210 − 42) ÷ 210 = 168 ÷ 210 = 0.80.

The criterion (low birthweight, yes/no) is binary, and the tool is used to classify. Predictive validity is therefore reported as sensitivity and specificity (and predictive values, or AUC for a continuous score), not a correlation (§16.2.3.2).
